stem: A client with chronic kidney disease is receiving epoetin alfa. Why should the nurse question a plan to use the ESA to target a hemoglobin level greater than 11 g/dL?

options.A: Higher hemoglobin targets with ESAs in chronic kidney disease are associated with greater risks of death, serious cardiovascular reactions, and stroke.
options.B: Hemoglobin targets above 11 g/dL eliminate cardiovascular risk and are preferred whenever anemia is present.
options.C: ESA safety is unrelated to the hemoglobin target, so escalating the dose has no clinically important downside.
options.D: The main serious complication of ESA therapy is hypoglycemia, which increases as hemoglobin approaches the normal range.

rationale: The current Epogen label carries a boxed warning for ESA-associated serious outcomes. In CKD trials, targeting hemoglobin above 11 g/dL increased risks of death, serious cardiovascular reactions, and stroke. The label directs clinicians to individualize dosing and use the lowest dose sufficient to reduce the need for RBC transfusions. A is therefore correct; B and C contradict the boxed warning, and D describes an adverse effect that is not the key ESA boxed-warning risk.
educational_objective: For CKD clients receiving epoetin alfa, recognize that targeting hemoglobin above 11 g/dL increases serious cardiovascular and mortality risk and that ESA dosing should use the lowest dose sufficient to reduce transfusion need.
source_organization: DailyMed / U.S. Food and Drug Administration labeling

source_original.stem: A client with chronic kidney disease receives an erythropoiesis-stimulating agent. Why should an unnecessarily high hemoglobin target be avoided?

options.A: Higher hemoglobin targets with ESAs can increase serious cardiovascular and thromboembolic risks
options.B: Higher hemoglobin targets eliminate cardiovascular risk and are preferred whenever anemia is present
options.C: ESA safety is unrelated to hemoglobin target, so dose escalation has no clinically important downside
options.D: The only important ESA complication is hypoglycemia, which increases as hemoglobin approaches normal

source_original.rationale: FDA boxed warnings for ESAs describe increased risks including death, myocardial infarction, stroke, and thromboembolism when used to target higher hemoglobin levels in CKD. Dosing should use the lowest dose sufficient to reduce transfusion needs.
source_original.source_detail: Boxed warning and CKD risk information for ESAs; cardiovascular, stroke, and thromboembolic risk with higher hemoglobin targets; accessed 2026-08-14.

correction_summary: Replaced the older general FDA safety page with the current June 2026 Epogen label, made the directly supported >11 g/dL threshold explicit, retained the lowest-dose principle, and reduced difficulty from hard to medium.

audit_findings.source_authority: Current DailyMed Epogen prescribing information; NCSBN 2026 Test Plan
audit_findings.claim_audit: The boxed warning and sections 2.2/5.1 directly support the >11 g/dL risk statement and lowest-dose strategy.

distractor_audit.D: Hypoglycemia is not the boxed-warning risk relevant to hemoglobin targeting.

audit_findings.ambiguity_second_answer: Only A explains why the specific >11 g/dL target should be questioned.
audit_findings.cueing: All alternatives address treatment risk/targeting; the key depends on label knowledge rather than wording.
audit_findings.blueprint: NCSBN p.12 Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies.
audit_findings.independent_second_pass: Rechecked the June 2026 boxed warning, CKD dosing section and 5.1, challenged the threshold and wording, and confirmed NCSBN p.12. A remained uniquely correct with no unsupported precision.
